title: Occupational Protection in Procedural Medicine: A Growing Multisociety Priority
summary: New multisociety guidelines highlight occupational protection, physician safety, radiation reduction, ergonomics, and workforce sustainability.
body_markdown:
For years, discussions about radiation safety in procedural medicine focused on awareness, monitoring, and compliance.


Today, the conversation is changing.


Earlier this year, the Cardiovascular and Interventional Radiological Society of Europe (CIRSE) and the Society of Interventional Radiology (SIR) released updated occupational protection guidelines, emphasizing that occupational safety extends beyond radiation exposure alone and must also address ergonomics, workplace injury, and the broader health of clinical teams.²


Recently, a coalition of leading cardiovascular and interventional societies—including SCAI, ACC, ASE, HRS, SIR, and SVS—published the[Expert Consensus Statement on Enhanced Radiation Protection: Time for Mandatory and Urgent Action](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13491342/) .¹


The title alone signals a cross-industry paradigm shift in thinking.


Occupational risks are no longer up for debate. The pressing challenge now is ensuring healthcare organizations take meaningful action to adopt and enforce enhanced protections for interventional teams. ****


## This Is Bigger Than Radiation Protection


While radiation exposure remains a central concern, both publications point to a broader reality: occupational safety in procedural medicine encompasses much more than just personal protective equipment (PPE).¹ ²


The updated CIRSE-SIR Occupational Protection Guideline specifically notes that occupational protection involves more than radiation protection and reflects growing awareness of the physical demands placed on physicians and staff working in procedural environments.²


The multisociety Expert Consensus Statement expands on that concern, highlighting long-term occupational challenges that include radiation exposure, cataracts, cancer risk, reproductive concerns, and musculoskeletal injuries associated with years of wearing heavy protective equipment.¹


These publications suggest a fundamental shift:


Physician safety is increasingly being viewed as a workforce issue, not just a safety issue.


## The Industry Is Moving Beyond Traditional Protection


The premise is straightforward: the best way to protect workers is not simply to provide better protective equipment, but to reduce or eliminate their exposure to hazards whenever possible.¹


For decades, procedural medicine has relied heavily on PPE. But today’s medical societies are increasingly encouraging healthcare organizations to look beyond traditional approaches and evaluate technologies that can reduce exposure at its source.¹


In simple terms, the goal is no longer just better protection.


The goal is less exposure.


## Rethinking Occupational Protection


The recent society publications do more than raise awareness—they call for action. As organizations evaluate ways to reduce occupational risks, there is a growing emphasis on engineering-based solutions that go beyond reliance on personal protective equipment alone.


This represents an important evolution in occupational protection. While traditional shielding and PPE remain essential, advances in medical technology create opportunities to address occupational hazards through changes in how procedures are performed, rather than relying exclusively on protective measures.


The[LIBERTY® Endovascular Robotic System](https://www.microbotmedical.com/liberty/) offers a different approach to occupational protection. LIBERTY enables physicians to perform procedures remotely from a seated position, up to 32 feet away from the procedure table, helping reduce occupational radiation exposure and physical strain.


This approach has the potential to support several priorities increasingly highlighted across the interventional community:


- **Reducing occupational radiation exposure** through remote operation away from the radiation source.
- **Addressing physical strain and fatigue** associated with prolonged standing and wearing heavy protective equipment.
- **Supporting long-term physician health and well-being** by helping reduce the cumulative occupational demands associated with interventional practice.


The growing emphasis on occupational protection signals an important shift in procedural medicine: physician safety must be a consideration in how interventional care continues to evolve. LIBERTY reflects this commitment by bringing physician protection to the forefront of endovascular innovation. As the industry looks toward the future, technologies like LIBERTY are helping advance a vision where improving patient care and protecting the physicians who deliver it go hand in hand.
